narrative:
The model estimated a 57% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is above even odds, so the application was denied on the prediction that failure was more likely than success—not because failure was certain.

The dominant reason was your third-year class standing. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This was the single strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your LSAT score of 31, below the accepted average of about 37, was the second most influential factor; despite that gap, it acted as a mild counterweight toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, below the accepted average of about 3.23, was third and also acted as a mild counterweight toward passing. Those two measures helped your case, but they did not outweigh the third-year standing. Gender and race were not used.

To proceed, ask admissions whether the denial can be reconsidered and what evidence would help. Supply any improved grades, a stronger LSAT retake, or proof of academic and bar-exam preparation. Ask about conditional admission, academic support, or a delayed reapplication plan, and consider addressing the third-year ranking directly with updated performance.
